claim: Ketamine and isoflurane are two widely used general anesthetics.
source: Ketamine (KET) and isoflurane (ISO) are two widely used general anesthetics, yet their distinct and shared neurophysiological mechanisms remain elusive.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical practice and common knowledge in anesthesiology.

claim: The distinct and shared neurophysiological mechanisms of ketamine and isoflurane remain elusive.
source: Ketamine (KET) and isoflurane (ISO) are two widely used general anesthetics, yet their distinct and shared neurophysiological mechanisms remain elusive.
evidence: This statement acknowledges gaps in current understanding, representing the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: KET activates a wide range of brain regions, notably in the cortical and subcortical nuclei involved in sensory, motor, emotional, and reward processing.
source: Our findings reveal that KET activates a wide range of brain regions, notably in the cortical and subcortical nuclei involved in sensory, motor, emotional, and reward processing, with the temporal association areas (TEa) as a strong hub, suggesting a top-down mechanism affecting consciousness by primarily targeting higher order cortical networks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental c-Fos expression data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The temporal association areas (TEa) serve as a strong hub in the ketamine-activated network.
source: Our findings reveal that KET activates a wide range of brain regions, notably in the cortical and subcortical nuclei involved in sensory, motor, emotional, and reward processing, with the temporal association areas (TEa) as a strong hub, suggesting a top-down mechanism affecting consciousness by primarily targeting higher order cortical networks.
evidence: This is based on network analysis of c-Fos expression data showing TEa as a hub node.

claim: Ketamine affects consciousness through a top-down mechanism by primarily targeting higher order cortical networks.
source: Our findings reveal that KET activates a wide range of brain regions, notably in the cortical and subcortical nuclei involved in sensory, motor, emotional, and reward processing, with the temporal association areas (TEa) as a strong hub, suggesting a top-down mechanism affecting consciousness by primarily targeting higher order cortical networks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, representing an inference from the observed activation patterns.

claim: ISO predominantly influences brain regions in the hypothalamus, impacting neuroendocrine control, autonomic function, and homeostasis.
source: In contrast, ISO predominantly influences brain regions in the hypothalamus, impacting neuroendocrine control, autonomic function, and homeostasis, with the locus coeruleus (LC) as a connector hub, indicating a bottom-up mechanism in anesthetic-induced unconsciousness.
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos expression data showing activation in hypothalamic regions.

claim: The locus coeruleus (LC) serves as a connector hub in the isoflurane-activated network.
source: In contrast, ISO predominantly influences brain regions in the hypothalamus, impacting neuroendocrine control, autonomic function, and homeostasis, with the locus coeruleus (LC) as a connector hub, indicating a bottom-up mechanism in anesthetic-induced unconsciousness.
evidence: This is based on network analysis identifying LC as a hub node in the ISO network.

claim: Isoflurane induces unconsciousness through a bottom-up mechanism.
source: In contrast, ISO predominantly influences brain regions in the hypothalamus, impacting neuroendocrine control, autonomic function, and homeostasis, with the locus coeruleus (LC) as a connector hub, indicating a bottom-up mechanism in anesthetic-induced unconsciousness.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, representing an inference from the observed activation patterns.

claim: KET and ISO both activate brain areas involved in sensory processing, memory and cognition, reward and motivation, as well as autonomic and homeostatic control.
source: KET and ISO both activate brain areas involved in sensory processing, memory and cognition, reward and motivation, as well as autonomic and homeostatic control, highlighting their shared effects on various neural pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos expression data showing co-activation of these regions by both anesthetics.

claim: At the molecular level, ketamine modulates neuronal excitability predominantly through N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors.
source: At the molecular level, ketamine (KET) modulates neuronal excitability predominantly through N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, whereas isoflurane (ISO) primarily affects gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABAa) receptors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ketamine's mechanism of action, supported by citation to Franks, 2008.

claim: Isoflurane primarily affects gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABAa) receptors.
source: At the molecular level, ketamine (KET) modulates neuronal excitability predominantly through N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, whereas isoflurane (ISO) primarily affects gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABAa) receptors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about isoflurane's mechanism of action, supported by citation to Franks, 2008.

claim: The distinct mechanisms of action of ketamine and isoflurane can each contribute to the loss of consciousness.
source: Their distinct mechanisms of action can each contribute to the loss of consciousness. (Franks, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Franks, 2008.

claim: The neural mechanisms of anesthetic induced unconsciousness involve both top-down and bottom-up processes.
source: In systems neuroscience, the neural mechanisms of anesthetic induced unconsciousness involve both top-down and bottom-up processes (Mashour, 2014; Mashour and Hudetz, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mashour, 2014 and Mashour and Hudetz, 2017.

claim: The top-down paradigm demonstrates that anesthetics induce unconsciousness by disrupting corticocortical and corticothalamic circuits responsible for neural information integration.
source: As evidenced by in vivo electrophysiology or functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies, the top-down paradigm demonstrates that anesthetics induce unconsciousness by disrupting corticocortical and corticothalamic circuits responsible for neural information integration, while peripheral sensory information can still be conveyed to the primary sensory cortex (Schroeder et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schroeder et al., 2016 and Lee et al., 2013.

claim: In the top-down paradigm, peripheral sensory information can still be conveyed to the primary sensory cortex during anesthesia.
source: As evidenced by in vivo electrophysiology or functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies, the top-down paradigm demonstrates that anesthetics induce unconsciousness by disrupting corticocortical and corticothalamic circuits responsible for neural information integration, while peripheral sensory information can still be conveyed to the primary sensory cortex (Schroeder et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schroeder et al., 2016 and Lee et al., 2013.

claim: The bottom-up approach involves the activation of sleep-promoting nuclei like ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) and inhibition of arousal centers in the brainstem and diencephalon.
source: The bottom-up approach, exemplified by ISO, involves the activation of sleep-promoting nuclei like ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) and inhibition of arousal centers in the brainstem and diencephalon, supporting the shared circuits of sleep and anesthesia (Moore et al., 2012; Nelson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moore et al., 2012 and Nelson et al., 2002.

claim: The bottom-up approach supports the shared circuits of sleep and anesthesia.
source: The bottom-up approach, exemplified by ISO, involves the activation of sleep-promoting nuclei like ventrolateral preoptic nucleus (VLPO) and inhibition of arousal centers in the brainstem and diencephalon, supporting the shared circuits of sleep and anesthesia (Moore et al., 2012; Nelson et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moore et al., 2012 and Nelson et al., 2002.

claim: Neuronal extracellular stimulation typically results in the elevation of adenosine 3',5'-cyclic monophosphate (cAMP) levels and calcium influx, ultimately leading to the upregulation of immediate early genes (IEGs) such as c-fos.
source: Neuronal extracellular stimulation typically results in the elevation of adenosine 3',5'-cyclic monophosphate (cAMP) levels and calcium influx, ultimately leading to the upregulation of immediate early genes (IEGs) such as c-fos (Yap and Greenberg, 2018; Morgan and Curran, 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yap and Greenberg, 2018 and Morgan and Curran, 1989.

claim: The translation product of c-fos, c-Fos protein, offers single-cell spatial resolution and has been utilized as a biomarker to identify anesthetic-activated brain regions.
source: The translation product of c-fos, c-Fos protein, offers single-cell spatial resolution and has been utilized as a biomarker to identify anesthetic-activated brain regions (Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2022.

claim: GABAergic agents inhibited cortical activity while concurrently activating subcortical brain regions, including VLPO, median preoptic nucleus (MEPO), lateral septal nucleus (LS), Edinger-Westphal nucleus (EW), and locus coeruleus (LC).
source: Previous investigations of c-Fos expression throughout the brain demonstrated that GABAergic agents inhibited cortical activity while concurrently activating subcortical brain regions, including VLPO, median preoptic nucleus (MEPO), lateral septal nucleus (LS), Edinger-Westphal nucleus (EW), and locus coeruleus (LC; Smith et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2008; Yatziv et al., 2020; Han et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Smith et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2008; Yatziv et al., 2020; Han et al., 2014.

claim: KET was shown to provoke wake-like c-Fos expression and intense augmentation of c-Fos expression in various brain regions at clinical dosages (75–100 mg/kg).
source: In contrast, KET was shown to provoke wake-like c-Fos expression and intense augmentation of c-Fos expression in various brain regions at clinical dosages (75–100 mg/kg; Lu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2008.

claim: The state of general anesthesia is not determined by activity in individual brain areas but emerges as a global change within the brain.
source: Moreover, it has been revealed that the state of general anesthesia is not determined by activity in individual brain areas but emerges as a global change within the brain.
evidence: This represents current understanding in the field about the nature of anesthetic-induced unconsciousness.

claim: The activation of lateral habenular nucleus (LHb), VLPO, supraoptic nucleus (SO), and central amygdaloid nucleus (CeA) are essential for anesthetic induced sedation, unconsciousness, or analgesia.
source: This change involves the activation of lateral habenular nucleus (LHb), VLPO, supraoptic nucleus (SO), and central amygdaloid nucleus (CeA), which are essential for anesthetic induced sedation, unconsciousness, or analgesia (Moore et al., 2012; Gelegen et al., 2018; Hua et al., 2020; Jiang-Xie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moore et al., 2012; Gelegen et al., 2018; Hua et al., 2020; Jiang-Xie et al., 2019.

claim: The administration of either KET or ISO elevated the EEG delta/theta power ratio while reducing EMG power.
source: Our results indicated that the administration of either KET or ISO elevated the EEG delta/theta power ratio while reducing EMG power (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that each drug induced a loss of consciousness.
evidence: This is supported by EEG and EMG data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The elevation of EEG delta/theta power ratio and reduction in EMG power suggest that each drug induced a loss of consciousness.
source: Our results indicated that the administration of either KET or ISO elevated the EEG delta/theta power ratio while reducing EMG power (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that each drug induced a loss of consciousness.
evidence: This is an inference from the EEG/EMG data, based on established understanding of these measures.

claim: KET elicited significant activation in almost all 53 brain regions when compared to the saline group.
source: Our findings revealed that KET elicited significant activation in almost all 53 brain regions when compared to the saline group.
evidence: This is based on Z-score analysis of c-Fos expression data.

claim: ISO showed substantial activation across various regions, excluding the cortical areas, when compared to the home cage group.
source: Conversely, ISO showed substantial activation across various regions, excluding the cortical areas, when compared to the home cage group (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on Z-score analysis of c-Fos expression data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: KET activated 141 out of a total of 201 brain regions compared to the saline group.
source: Compared to the saline group, KET activated 141 out of a total of 201 brain regions (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of c-Fos expression data presented in Figure 2.

claim: KET activated sensory areas, such as visual areas (VIS), auditory areas (AUD), somatosensory areas (SS), gustatory areas (GU), and higher-order cortical areas.
source: Notably, KET activated sensory areas, such as visual areas (VIS), auditory areas (AUD), somatosensory areas (SS), gustatory areas (GU), and higher-order cortical areas, including the anterior cingulate area (ACA), temporal association areas (TEa), retrosplenial area (RSP), and dorsal peduncular area (DP).
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data showing activation in these regions.

claim: KET's activation of sensory and cortical areas contrasts with the usual inhibiting effect of anesthetics on these neural circuits.
source: This contrasts with the usual inhibiting effect of anesthetics on these neural circuits and suggests the unique ability of KET to sustain certain neuronal circuits in an active state (Brown et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of established knowledge, supported by citation to Brown et al., 2011.

claim: KET's impact on the olfactory system was distinct compared to other types of general anesthetics.
source: Furthermore, its impact on the olfactory system, involving key structures such as the anterior olfactory nucleus (AON), main olfactory bulb (MOB), olfactory tubercle (OT), perirhinal area (PERI), piriform area (PIR), and ectorhinal area (ECT), was distinct compared to other types of general anesthetics (Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data and comparison with literature, supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2020.

claim: KET affected emotional and reward processing regions such as the nucleus accumbens (ACB), orbital area (ORB), infralimbic area (ILA), and prelimbic area (PL).
source: Moreover, KET affected emotional and reward processing regions such as the nucleus accumbens (ACB; Floresco, 2015), orbital area (ORB; Rolls et al., 2020), infralimbic area (ILA), and prelimbic area (PL; Pfarr et al., 2018), suggesting an impact on the circuitry responsible for modulating reward and affective states.
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data, with functional interpretations supported by citations to Floresco, 2015; Rolls et al., 2020; Pfarr et al., 2018.

claim: The thalamus, including the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT) and lateral group of the dorsal thalamus (LAT), showed enhanced activity under the influence of KET.
source: The thalamus, including the paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (PVT) (Ren et al., 2018) and lateral group of the dorsal thalamus (LAT) (Suzuki and Larkum, 2020), which are vital in arousal regulation, also showed enhanced activity under the influence of KET.
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data, with functional interpretations supported by citations to Ren et al., 2018 and Suzuki and Larkum, 2020.

claim: Hindbrain regions under KET anesthesia, including the magnocellular reticular nucleus (MARN), paragigantocellular reticular nucleus (PGRN), lateral reticular nucleus (LRN), nucleus raphe obscurus (RO), and sublaterodorsal nucleus (SLD), showed notable activity.
source: Hindbrain regions under KET anesthesia, including the magnocellular reticular nucleus (MARN), paragigantocellular reticular nucleus (PGRN), lateral reticular nucleus (LRN), nucleus raphe obscurus (RO), and sublaterodorsal nucleus (SLD), showed notable activity.
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data.

claim: The activation in regions like PGRN and SLD suggests that KET modulates brain regions critical for the regulation of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep.
source: In particular, the activation in regions like PGRN and SLD suggests that KET modulates brain regions critical for the regulation of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep (Goutagny et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference from the c-Fos data, supported by citation to Goutagny et al., 2008.

claim: ISO predominantly influences the hypothalamus, a key area for neuroendocrine regulation, autonomic control, and homeostasis.
source: The activation of these regions suggested a substantial influence of ISO on hypothalamic regulation, including neuroendocrine control, autonomic function, and homeostasis (Gu et al., 1999; Adamantidis and de Lecea, 2023).
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data showing activation in hypothalamic regions, with functional interpretations supported by citations to Gu et al., 1999 and Adamantidis and de Lecea, 2023.

claim: ISO affected the areas governing circadian rhythms and sleep-wake regulation, as indicated by activation in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCH) and subparaventricular zone (SBPV).
source: Additionally, ISO affected the areas governing circadian rhythms and sleep-wake regulation, as indicated by activation in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCH) and subparaventricular zone (SBPV; Lu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data, with functional interpretations supported by citation to Lu et al., 2001.

claim: Sensory processing and reward circuitry, including the OT, SI, and ACB, demonstrated significant activation under ISO.
source: Moreover, sensory processing and reward circuitry, including the OT (Giessel and Datta, 2014), SI (Cui et al., 2022), and ACB (Zhou et al., 2022), demonstrated significant activation.
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data, with functional interpretations supported by citations to Giessel and Datta, 2014; Cui et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2022.

claim: Activation of the perirhinal area (PERI) and nucleus of reuniens (RE) pointed to a potential impact on cognitive processes and memory systems under ISO.
source: Activation of the perirhinal area (PERI; Yang and Naya, 2023), and nucleus of reuniens (RE; Huang et al., 2021) pointed to a potential impact on cognitive processes and memory systems.
evidence: This is an inference from c-Fos expression data, supported by citations to Yang and Naya, 2023 and Huang et al., 2021.

claim: ISO activates the EW, a finding that aligned with observations under sevoflurane anesthesia.
source: Our study also revealed ISO activates the EW, a finding that aligned with observations under sevoflurane anesthesia (Yi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data, with comparison to literature supported by citation to Yi et al., 2023.

claim: The bed nuclei of the stria terminalis (BST), associated with stress responses and emotional regulation, exhibited significant activation under ISO.
source: The bed nuclei of the stria terminalis (BST), associated with stress responses and emotional regulation, exhibited significant activation (Daniel and Rainnie, 2016).
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data, with functional interpretation supported by citation to Daniel and Rainnie, 2016.

claim: 43 brain regions are co-activated by KET and ISO.
source: A Venn diagram displays 43 brain regions co-activated by KET and ISO, identified by the adjusted p-values (p<0.05) for both KET and ISO.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of c-Fos expression data, as shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The co-activation of the PIR, ENT, and OT by KET and ISO points to changes in sensory perception typical of anesthetics.
source: Examples of these effects include impacts on sensory processing, as evidenced by the activation of the PIR, ENT (Chapuis et al., 2013), and OT (Giessel and Datta, 2014), pointing to changes in sensory perception typical of anesthetics.
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data showing co-activation, with functional interpretations supported by citations to Chapuis et al., 2013 and Giessel and Datta, 2014.

claim: Memory and cognitive functions are influenced by KET and ISO, as indicated by the activation of the subiculum (SUB), dentate gyrus (DG), and RE.
source: Memory and cognitive functions are influenced, as indicated by the activation of the subiculum (SUB; Roy et al., 2017), dentate gyrus (DG; Sun et al., 2020), and RE (Huang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data showing co-activation, with functional interpretations supported by citations to Roy et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2021.

claim: The reward and motivational systems are engaged by KET and ISO, involving the ACB and ventral tegmental area (VTA).
source: The reward and motivational systems are engaged, involving the ACB and ventral tegmental area (VTA), signaling the modulation of reward pathways (Al-Hasani et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data showing co-activation, with functional interpretation supported by citation to Al-Hasani et al., 2021.

claim: Autonomic and homeostatic control are affected by KET and ISO, as shown by areas like the lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) and medial preoptic area (MPO).
source: Autonomic and homeostatic control are also affected, as shown by areas like the lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) (Mickelsen et al., 2019) and medial preoptic area (MPO) (McGinty and Szymusiak, 1990), emphasizing effects on functions such as feeding and thermoregulation.
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data showing co-activation, with functional interpretations supported by citations to Mickelsen et al., 2019 and McGinty and Szymusiak, 1990.

claim: Stress and arousal responses are impacted by KET and ISO through the activation of the paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus (PVH) and LC.
source: Stress and arousal responses are impacted through the activation of the paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus (PVH) (Rasiah et al., 2023; Islam et al., 2022) and LC (Ross and Van Bockstaele, 2020).
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data showing co-activation, with functional interpretations supported by citations to Rasiah et al., 2023; Islam et al., 2022; Ross and Van Bockstaele, 2020.

claim: KET administration elicited a significant activation in a broad array of brain regions, with cluster 4 displaying the most substantial upregulation in expression.
source: KET administration elicited a significant activation in a broad array of brain regions, with cluster 4 displaying the most substantial upregulation in expression.
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis of c-Fos expression data.

claim: Cluster 4 in KET hierarchical clustering incorporates cortical areas and cerebral nuclei that are integral for motor coordination and motivational behaviors.
source: This cluster incorporates cortical areas, including the visceral area (VISC), GU, ORB, somatomotor areas (MO), ACA, and SS, and cerebral nuclei that are integral for motor coordination and motivational behaviors, specifically, the dorsolateral and ventrolateral pallidum (PALd, PALv) and striatum (STRd, STRv) (Grillner et al., 2005, Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis, with functional interpretation supported by citation to Grillner et al., 2005.

claim: No significantly inhibited brain regions were detected in the ISO group.
source: No significantly inhibited brain regions were detected in the ISO group (as no Z value fell below –2); clusters 3 and 4 expression levels were similar to or lower than those in the control group, with cluster 3 having a mean Z value of 0.27 and cluster 4 a mean Z value of –1.1, as shown in Figure 5D and E.
evidence: This is based on Z-score analysis of c-Fos expression data presented in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The most pronounced upregulation of ISO-induced c-Fos expression was observed in cluster 2, which includes brain regions responsible for a variety of functions.
source: The most pronounced upregulation of ISO-induced c-Fos expression was observed in the second cluster (mean Z value = 4.7), which includes brain regions responsible for a variety of functions: the periventricular zone (PVZ) and lateral zone (LZ) of the hypothalamus, vital for endocrine and autonomic system regulation Gu et al., 1999; the ventral striatum (STRv), pallidum (PAL), and lateral septal complex (LSX) of the striatum, key areas in reward and motivation Cox and Witten, 2019; the taenia tecta (TT), PIR, essential for olfactory processing (Bekkers and Suzuki, 2013; Kataoka et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis of c-Fos expression data, with functional interpretations supported by multiple citations.

claim: ISO demonstrates a more concentrated influence on brain activity with consistently higher clustering quality and fewer clusters than KET.
source: ISO demonstrates a more concentrated influence on brain activity with consistently higher clustering quality and fewer clusters than KET, suggesting a focused impact on specific brain functions (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis comparing KET and ISO, as shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: In the hierarchical clustering analysis of KET exposure, cluster 5 showed the most significant activation and is composed mainly of cortical and striatal regions crucial for sensory processing, spatial memory, reward, and cognitive functions.
source: Cluster 5, showing the most significant activation, is composed mainly of the cortical and striatal regions crucial for sensory processing, spatial memory, reward, and cognitive functions (Haber, 2016).
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis of c-Fos expression data, with functional interpretation supported by citation to Haber, 2016.

claim: ISO hierarchical clustering identified cluster 3 exhibiting the highest mean Z value of 7.27, which encompasses the SO, VLPO, TU, and CEA.
source: ISO hierarchical clustering identified three distinct clusters, with cluster 3 exhibiting the highest mean Z value of 7.27. This cluster encompasses the SO, VLPO, TU, and CEA (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis of c-Fos expression data presented in Figure 6E.

claim: The SO, VLPO, and CEA have been previously reported to play critical roles in the mechanisms of anesthesia.
source: Notably, the SO, VLPO, and CEA have been previously reported to play critical roles in the mechanisms of anesthesia (Moore et al., 2012; Hua et al., 2020; Jiang-Xie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moore et al., 2012; Hua et al., 2020; Jiang-Xie et al., 2019.

claim: Cluster 1 in ISO hierarchical clustering showed a relative decrease in expression, indicating that nearly half of the brain areas had reduced c-Fos expression compared to the control group.
source: Cluster 1 showed a relative decrease in expression (n=91, mean Z value: –0.54), indicating that nearly half of the brain areas had reduced c-Fos expression compared to the control group.
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis of c-Fos expression data.

claim: Correlation analysis revealed similar network connectivity and densities between the ISO and home cage groups.
source: Correlation analysis revealed similar network connectivity and densities between the ISO and home cage groups (mean interregional correlations: Fisher Z=–0.018, p=0.98; network densities: 0.10 vs 0.09).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of c-Fos expression data.

claim: KET significantly increased network density and mean interregional correlations compared to the saline group.
source: In contrast, KET significantly increased network density (0.46 vs 0.06) and mean interregional correlations compared to the saline group (Fisher Z=3.54, p<0.001; Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), indicating enhanced interregional correlation with KET administration.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of c-Fos expression data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The LC is characterized by its high degree and eigenvector centrality, as well as its notably higher betweenness centrality, underscoring its pivotal role in propagating and integrating neural signals within the ISO-influenced network.
source: The LC, characterized by its high degree and eigenvector centrality, as well as its notably higher betweenness centrality (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) underscores its pivotal role in propagating and integrating neural signals within the ISO-influenced network.
evidence: This is based on network analysis of c-Fos expression data, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the KET group, the TEa serves as a hub, emphasizing its integrative role in KET-induced dissociative anesthesia.
source: In the KET group, the TEa serves as a hub, emphasizing its integrative role in KET-induced dissociative anesthesia.
evidence: This is based on network analysis of c-Fos expression data.

claim: The emergence of consciousness results from active and coherent connections and communication among various brain regions, enabling global information availability and integration within a neural network.
source: Studies utilizing functional MRI, PET scans, EEG, and computational modeling have indicated that the emergence of consciousness results from active and coherent connections and communication among various brain regions, enabling global information availability and integration within a neural network (Lamme, 2006; Dehaene and Changeux, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lamme, 2006 and Dehaene and Changeux, 2011.

claim: A significant activation throughout the cortex-dominated brain following KET administration was accompanied by a notable increase in network density.
source: Our findings revealed a significant activation throughout the cortex-dominated brain following KET administration, accompanied by a notable increase in network density (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression and network analysis data presented in Figure 7A.

claim: The observed hyperactivity and heightened functional connectivity under KET could potentially compromise the effective integration of information within the network, possibly leading to the loss of consciousness.
source: The observed hyperactivity and heightened functional connectivity could potentially compromise the effective integration of information within the network, possibly leading to the loss of consciousness.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: KET preferentially inhibits GABAergic interneurons through NMDA receptor mediation, leading to abnormal excitatory activity in the cortex and limbic system and potentially disrupting consciousness.
source: This finding aligns with previous studies which indicate that KET preferentially inhibits GABAergic interneurons through NMDA receptor mediation, leading to abnormal excitatory activity in the cortex and limbic system and potentially disrupting consciousness (Seamans, 2008; Brown et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Seamans, 2008 and Brown et al., 2010.

claim: The LC plays a pivotal role in regulating vigilance, as well as respiratory and cardiovascular responses.
source: The LC, which is the primary source of noradrenaline in the brain, plays a pivotal role in regulating vigilance, as well as respiratory and cardiovascular responses (Magalhães et al., 2018; Wood and Valentino, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Magalhães et al., 2018 and Wood and Valentino, 2017.

claim: During ISO anesthesia, key autonomic functions are typically suppressed, including the regulation of normal body temperature, respiration, blood pressure, and heart rate.
source: During ISO anesthesia, key autonomic functions are typically suppressed, including the regulation of normal body temperature, respiration, blood pressure, and heart rate (Skovsted and Sapthavichaikul, 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Skovsted and Sapthavichaikul, 1977.

claim: The activation of the LC during the administration of ISO may act as a compensatory mechanism to maintain a necessary level of autonomic response.
source: In this context, the activation of the LC during the administration of ISO may act as a compensatory mechanism to maintain a necessary level of autonomic response.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the LC activation observed under ISO.

claim: Activation of the LC during ISO anesthesia can have a wake-promoting effect.
source: While it is known that activation of the LC during ISO anesthesia can have a wake-promoting effect (Vazey and Aston-Jones, 2014), this phenomenon might contribute to a balance between inducing loss of consciousness and preserving essential autonomic functions during anesthesia.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Vazey and Aston-Jones, 2014.

claim: c-Fos expression is significantly higher in the KET group compared to the ISO group, and in the saline group compared to the home cage group.
source: Our results demonstrate that c-Fos expression is significantly higher in the KET group compared to the ISO group, and in the saline group compared to the home cage group, as shown in Figures 2 and 3.
evidence: This is based on c-Fos expression data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Intraperitoneal injections in the saline and KET groups might still elicit pain and stress responses in mice despite 4 days of acclimation.
source: Despite 4 days of acclimation, including handling and injections, intraperitoneal injections in the saline and KET groups might still elicit pain and stress responses in mice.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of potential confounding factors.

claim: Adult male wild-type (WT) mice (C57BL/6J; 8–10 weeks old, weight from 22 to 26 g) were used in the experiments.
source: Adult male wild-type (WT) mice (C57BL/6J; 8–10 weeks old, weight from 22 to 26 g) were purchased from institute-approved vendors (LingChang Experiment Animal Co., China).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects used in the study.

claim: Mice were individually housed and maintained on a 12 hr:12 hr light/dark cycle with lights on at 07:00 a.m. and off at 07:00 p.m.
source: Mice were individually housed and maintained on a 12 hr:12 hr light/dark cycle (lights on at 07:00 a.m. and off at 07:00 p.m.) with food and water available ad libitum.
evidence: This describes the housing conditions for the experimental animals.

claim: All experiments were conducted between 13:00 and 14:30 (ZT6–ZT7.5).
source: All experiments were conducted between 13:00 and 14:30 (ZT6–ZT7.5).
evidence: This describes the timing of experimental procedures.

claim: For 90 min after KET injection or ISO inhalation, mice were deeply anesthetized with 5% ISO and transcardially perfused.

claim: Coronal sections (50 µm) of the whole brain were cut using a cryostat after being embedded with OCT compound and freezing.

claim: The depth of anesthesia was evaluated based on the power ratio of the EEG signals within the delta (0.5–4 Hz) and theta (6–10 Hz) frequency bands, combined with the changes in the EMG.
source: The depth of anesthesia was evaluated based on the power ratio of the EEG signals within the delta (0.5–4 Hz) and theta (6–10 Hz) frequency bands, combined with the changes in the EMG (Luo et al., 2023).
evidence: This describes the methodology for assessing anesthesia depth, supported by citation to Luo et al., 2023.

claim: One out of every three brain slices (100 µm intervals) of each whole brain was used for immunohistochemistry.
source: One out of every three brain slices (100 µm intervals) of each whole brain was washed three times with 0.1 M phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 10 min and permeabilized for 30 min at room temperature with 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS (PBST).
evidence: This describes the sampling strategy for immunohistochemistry.

source: A custom-written software package was employed for cellular quantification within brain images. The software consists of three components: atlas rotation, image registration, and signal detection.

claim: Hierarchical clustering was performed by first computing the pairwise Euclidean distances among brain regions.
source: After normalizing the data, we performed hierarchical clustering by first computing the pairwise Euclidean distances among brain regions.
